analysis.one_liner: Requires electronics makers to share repair manuals, parts, and tools with independent repair shops and owners.
analysis.headline: The right-to-repair bill had a Democratic sponsor and cosponsors from both parties, but the Senate Commerce Committee never held a hearing or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require manufacturers of digital electronic equipment — phones, laptops, appliances, farm machinery — to sell documentation, parts, and repair tools to independent repair shops and equipment owners on the same terms they offer their own authorized repair networks. It excludes cars, trucks, and medical devices, and it gives the Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general the power to enforce the requirement. It was introduced in March 2022, sent to the Senate Commerce Committee, and never received a hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Owners of electronics and equipment who want to fix their own devices or choose a local repair shop instead of being pushed back to the manufacturer or its authorized dealers. Independent repair businesses gain access to the manuals, parts, and diagnostic software that manufacturers currently keep in-house, letting them compete for repair work. Farmers and small equipment operators benefit because farm equipment is covered even though cars and trucks are not.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Device owners and independent repair shops

how_it_helps.text: Requires manufacturers to make documentation, parts, and tools — including software needed to pair parts and calibrate repairs — available to owners and independent repair providers on fair and reasonable terms, defined as no worse than the best terms offered to authorized repair providers [S2][S3].

For equipment with electronic security locks, manufacturers must provide what is needed to disable and reset those locks during a repair, so owners are not locked out of fixing products they own [S3].
Enforcement is available through the Federal Trade Commission and through state attorneys general, who can seek injunctions, civil penalties, and restitution for state residents [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Electronics, appliance, and equipment manufacturers bear the cost of opening up parts, documentation, and tools — revenue they currently capture through their own repair networks and by steering customers to buy new devices instead of repairing old ones. Some of that cost could show up in device prices, and manufacturers argue it weakens their control over product security and trade secrets.

drawbacks.text: The bill explicitly requires manufacturers to provide the tools and codes needed to disable electronic security locks, which manufacturers and security researchers have warned can weaken built-in protections against hacking and tampering [S3].

It exempts motor vehicle makers, dealers, and medical device manufacturers entirely, so the car repairs and hospital equipment repairs where restricted-repair problems are well documented stay out of reach [S3].

Manufacturers would face compliance costs in maintaining public parts catalogs and tools, and critics note trade-secret protection is preserved only 'as necessary' to provide the required materials, leaving room for disputes over what must be disclosed [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and direct: cheaper, faster repairs and less pressure to replace devices when a fix would do. The main honest concerns are around security lockouts and the burden on smaller manufacturers, though the bill preserves trade secrets except where disclosure is needed to complete a repair. The biggest design weakness is what it leaves out — cars and medical devices — which shrinks the public benefit considerably.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee in March 2022, and the committee never took it up, so it died when that Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Sen. Ben Ray Luján introduced the Fair Repair Act on March 14, 2022, with Sens. Cynthia Lummis and Ron Wyden as the only cosponsors [S1][S3][S4].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation, which was the only action it ever received [S5].
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action followed, and the bill expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Electronics and equipment manufacturers came out ahead: without the bill, they keep exclusive control of parts, repair documentation, and diagnostic tools, and the repair market stays tilted toward their own authorized channels. Independent repair shops and device owners remain in the position the bill would have changed.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — a Democrat sponsored and the two cosponsors were one Democrat (Wyden) and one Republican (Lummis) — but the bill drew only two cosponsors out of 100 senators and never reached a vote, so no roll-call record exists.

industries.note: Companies like phone and laptop makers currently channel repairs through their own or authorized networks, using parts pairing and restricted tools. The bill would force them to share parts, manuals, and tools on equal terms, cutting into repair revenue and new-device sales driven by unrepairable products.

Farm equipment is digital electronic equipment under the bill's definitions, and only street-certified motor vehicles are excluded, so tractor and machinery makers would have to open up diagnostics and parts that independent mechanics currently cannot get.

These businesses would gain access on equal terms to the documentation, parts, and diagnostic tools needed to repair modern electronics, allowing them to compete for work now reserved for authorized networks.
The bill exempts them entirely, so they keep the status quo in which hospitals and clinics depend on manufacturer-controlled service for device repair.
